awd_abstract_narration:
This award will provide support for the 2025 RNA Editing Gordon Research Seminar (GRS) entitled “Biological Discoveries and Emerging Technologies in RNA Modifications and Editing” to be held in Lucca (Barga), Italy, on March 15–16, 2025. Organized by and for early-career researchers, this GRS will provide a dedicated forum for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers to present their ongoing work, share ideas, and develop professional skills before the associated Gordon Research Conference (GRC) on RNA Editing. All attending trainees will have the opportunity to present their research in either an oral or poster format and will benefit from mentorship opportunities including a keynote lecture from a prominent leader in the field and a panel focused on developing scientific writing skills. The GRS aims to promote scientific exchange, mentorship, community building, and fostering an inclusive environment. By offering early-career researchers the opportunity to share unpublished findings and connect with their peers, the GRS will support the development of the next generation of scientific leaders and innovators in RNA biology. 

RNA modifications and editing are essential to gene regulation, impacting key processes like translation, immunity, and disease progression. While these modifications are present in nearly all organisms, many of their biological functions remain poorly understood. The 2025 GRS will highlight emerging discoveries in two sessions, “RNA Modifications Across Biological Systems” and “Tools and Technologies in RNA Editing and Modifications.” These sessions will emphasize fundamental discoveries and technological advances with a focus on presenting unpublished data to inspire scientific exchange and interdisciplinary collaboration. By providing a space for early-career researchers to network and develop scientific and professional skills, this seminar will advance research in RNA biology and contribute to the development of tools and technologies with applications in health, biotechnology, and agriculture.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The 2025 RNA Editing Gordon Research Seminar (GRS) brought together early-career scientists from around the world to share and discuss new discoveries in RNA editing that affect cellular function in both health and disease. Once viewed as just an intermediate between DNA and protein, RNA has been recognized as a biomolecule that can be chemically modified in ways that influence numerous biological processes. During this two-day seminar, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers presented their recent, unpublished findings and technological advancements in the field of RNA editing and modifications. This seminar's focus on both biological discoveries and the development of novel technologies enabled the advancement of our understanding of RNA editing and highlighted emerging tools that may ultimately contribute to improved methods for characterization, diagnostics, and therapeutics.

In addition to advancing scientific exchange, this GRS played a critical role in supporting the professional development of the next generation of researchers. The meeting was composed of 62 participants from North America, Europe, and Asia, the majority of whom were graduate students and postdoctoral fellows. Many of these trainees went on to participate in the associated 2025 RNA Editing Gordon Research Conference (GRC) as well. All attendees had the opportunity to present their work through oral presentations or poster sessions, creating an environment where early-career researchers were the main contributors. Mentorship was a key component of the program, including a keynote lecture and panel discussion focused on scientific writing and communication, both of which are critical skills for sharing research with scientific and general audiences. These sessions demystified the process of publishing and grant writing and empowered trainees to communicate their work more effectively.

This seminar also had broader impacts by fostering a collaborative and inclusive scientific community. Support from the National Science Foundation reduced financial barriers to participation, enabling a diverse group of trainees to attend and engage in international scientific exchange. The GRS created a space for networking, generating ideas, and forming new collaborations in a supportive environment. Feedback from the participants emphasized the value of interactive discussions and connecting with peers at similar career stages. By bringing together emerging scientists, the 2025 RNA Editing GRS helped build a more connected, diverse, and well-prepared research community. Continued dissemination of ideas and collaborations formed at this seminar are anticipated to contribute to future scientific advances and publications in the field of RNA editing.
